lesson.title: Outsmarting RuBisCO by Splitting the Job in Two
lesson.summary: C4 plants avoid most photorespiration by fixing carbon dioxide in one cell type using a different enzyme, then shuttling the carbon to a separate, oxygen-poor cell type where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle operate.
lesson.body:
The core problem behind photorespiration, covered in the previous chapter, is that RuBisCO sometimes grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, especially when a C3 leaf's internal oxygen concentration climbs relative to carbon dioxide under hot, dry conditions. C4 plants solve this not by building a better RuBisCO, but by changing the surroundings RuBisCO operates in, so that it almost never encounters a low carbon dioxide, high oxygen environment in the first place.

The trick relies on a division of labor between two cell types arranged in a distinctive ring pattern around the leaf's veins, called Kranz anatomy. In the outer mesophyll cells, carbon dioxide is fixed not by RuBisCO but by a different enzyme, PEP carboxylase, which attaches it to a three-carbon molecule called phosphoenolpyruvate to form the four-carbon compound oxaloacetate, the source of the name C4. PEP carboxylase has no oxygenase side reaction at all and binds carbon dioxide, in the form of bicarbonate, far more tightly than RuBisCO does, so it keeps fixing carbon efficiently even when carbon dioxide levels inside the leaf are relatively low.

That four-carbon compound, typically converted to malate, is then transported through small channels called plasmodesmata into neighboring bundle-sheath cells, which sit closer to the vein and are largely sealed off from the leaf's air spaces. There, the four-carbon molecule is broken back down, releasing a concentrated burst of carbon dioxide right next to RuBisCO, which in C4 plants is essentially confined to these bundle-sheath chloroplasts. That local concentration of carbon dioxide is high enough to keep RuBisCO's active site heavily favoring its carboxylase reaction over its oxygenase reaction, so the Calvin cycle can run in this protected, oxygen-poor pocket with photorespiration suppressed to a small fraction of what a C3 plant would experience under the same conditions.

This strategy is not free. Regenerating the phosphoenolpyruvate spent in the mesophyll cells costs additional ATP beyond what the Calvin cycle itself requires, so C4 photosynthesis is more energetically expensive per carbon dioxide molecule fixed than the plain C3 pathway. In cool or shaded environments, that extra cost outweighs the benefit, which is part of why C4 plants have not simply replaced C3 plants everywhere. But in hot, bright, and often drought-prone habitats, where a C3 plant would be closing its stomata and bleeding sugar to photorespiration, the C4 strategy more than pays for itself.

Corn, sugarcane, and sorghum are well-known C4 crops, and their productivity in hot climates is a direct, visible consequence of this carbon-concentrating mechanism. C4 photosynthesis is a striking example of convergent evolution, since the underlying biochemical toolkit, PEP carboxylase, the four-carbon shuttle molecules, and Kranz anatomy, arose independently multiple times across unrelated plant lineages, all converging on the same basic fix to the same underlying RuBisCO problem.
